title: Your Agent Boots. Phoenix Still Doesn’t Know It Exists.
author: Daniel
summary: A MatrixOS agent can start, emit a beacon, and do useful work—while Phoenix’s swarm workspace still has no idea it exists. That is not a mysterious boot failure. It is usually a missing contract between two projects. The agent source defines what the process does. Phoenix’s per-agent metadata file tells the workspace how to find, configure, constrain, and present that agent. Leave out either half and you get the software equivalent of an operator arriving at the gate with a working radio and no badge. The radio is excellent. The gate remains unimpressed. This walkthrough follows the real layout: an agent package in MatrixOS, a JSON manifest in Phoenix, and optional configuration editors and custom panels. We’ll also look at how Phoenix treats signing and certificate requirements, so nobody puts a private key in a JSON file and calls it “automation.” Two projects, two jobs Keep the responsibilities separate: MatrixOS repository └── agents/python_core/shift_scribe/ ├── __init__.py └── shift_scribe.py # runtime behavior Phoenix repository ├── agents_meta/shift_scribe.json # workspace contract and defaults └── matrix_gui/ ├── swarm_workspace/cls_lib/agent/config_editors/ │ └── shift_scribe.py # optional configuration dialog └── core/panel/custom_panels/shift_scribe/ └── status_panel.py # optional custom controls The metadata file belongs to the agent type, not to each swarm instance. Phoenix reads the JSON files in agents_meta to populate the agent palette. When you add an agent to a workspace, its defaults become the starting configuration for that node; the workspace then saves the operator’s edits. 1. Start with the MatrixOS source skeleton Create a package whose folder and Python module share the agent’s snake_case name. The environment path setup must run before imports from the MatrixOS tree. Guard each environment value: os.getenv() can return None, and sys.path.insert(0, None) is not a fun way to begin a mission. Here is a small scaffold based on the supplied template. It includes the mixin import that the original snippet needs, and uses consistent spaces: import os import sys for env_name in ( " SITE_ROOT " , " AGENT_PATH " ): env_path = os . getenv ( env_name ) if env_path and env_path not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , env_path ) from core.python_core.boot_agent import BootAgent from core.python_core.mixin.reflex_alert import ReflexAlertMixin from core.python_core.utils.swarm_sleep import interruptible_sleep from core.python_core.class_lib.packet_delivery.utility.encryption.utility import ( identity , ) IdentityObject = identity . IdentityObject class Agent ( BootAgent , ReflexAlertMixin ): def __init__ ( self ): super (). __init__ () self . AGENT_VERSION = " 1.0.0 " # BootAgent loads the directive in super(). cfg = self . tree_node . get ( " config " , {}) self . report_role = cfg . get ( " report_to_role " , " hive.forensics.data_feed " ) self . alert_role = cfg . get ( " alert_to_role " , " hive.rpc " ) self . interval = int ( cfg . get ( " interval " , 30 )) # Monitor the worker thread. self . _emit_beacon = self . check_for_thread_poke ( " worker " , timeout = 60 , emit_to_file_interval = 10 ) def worker_pre ( self ): self . log ( " Shift Scribe on station. " ) def post_boot ( self ): self . log ( " Shift Scribe booted. Ready. " ) def worker ( self , config : dict = None , identity : IdentityObject = None , ): cfg = config or self . tree_node . get ( " config " , {}) self . _emit_beacon () self . log ( " Worker cycle complete. " ) interval = int ( cfg . get ( " interval " , self . interval )) interruptible_sleep ( self , interval ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : agent = Agent () agent . boot () The bootstrap and imports are the load-bearing part of the source contract. Keep lifecycle methods and the worker(config, identity) signature in the shape expected by the MatrixOS runtime. BootAgent provides the loaded tree_node; read this agent’s settings from its config, then supply sensible fallbacks. Use interruptible_sleep for a recurring worker so the runtime can stop it cleanly. Emit a beacon for the actual worker thread you want monitored. The sample you supplied also imports threading, datetime, and OrderedDict. Add those only when the implementation uses them. Python will not award extra professionalism points for unused imports. If a class inherits from ReflexAlertMixin, import it; otherwise the class definition will fail before the first log line gets its moment in the sun. The example worker is intentionally boring in the productive way: it reads configuration, reports liveness, does one cycle, and sleeps. Replace the log line with the agent’s job. Add dedicated threads only when the work needs them, and give each monitored thread its own beacon. 2. Add the Phoenix meta-file Create agents_meta/shift_scribe.json. The filename stem and the name should match exactly; Phoenix uses that name to find the manifest and the runtime package. Here is a starter manifest: { "name" : "shift_scribe" , "universal_id" : "shift-scribe" , "constraints" : [ { "packet_signing" : { "in" : true , "out" : true } } ], "config" : { "ui" : { "agent_tree" : { "emoji" : "🧭" } }, "interval" : 30 , "report_to_role" : "hive.forensics.data_feed" , "alert_to_role" : "hive.rpc" } } The top-level fields have distinct jobs: name is the stable agent-type name used by Phoenix’s palette and module lookup. Keep it aligned with the MatrixOS folder and module. universal_id is useful metadata, but a workspace node gets its own runtime identity when it is added. Don’t hard-code one live swarm instance ID into a reusable agent type. constraints declares requirements the workspace must resolve. Phoenix checks that a constraint has a registered editor or auto-generation handler; an unknown name is not a wish Phoenix can grant. config holds defaults and Phoenix UI hints. The workspace copies these into a new node, and the agent reads the operational values from its directive. The little compass under config.ui.agent_tree.emoji is the return icon: it labels the agent in the palette/tree. Pick an emoji that survives your terminal font and looks different from the other thirty-seven shields. 3. Let constraints provision security material Phoenix’s constraints are more than badges. They tell the workspace and deployment path what resources an agent needs. For example, the real matrix_https metadata declares packet signing in both directions, a connection certificate, and HTTPS transport: "constraints" : [ { "packet_signing" : { "in" : true , "out" : true } }, { "connection_cert" : {} }, { "https" : {} } ] If the agent needs to phone home to Phoenix, give it a signing key pair. In this metadata, packet_signing in and out are both enabled: the agent needs its private signing key for outbound packets and the appropriate public key to verify inbound traffic. Phoenix’s registered packet_signing auto-generation handler creates the key material during deployment and injects only the fields required by the directive. The connection-certificate handler can likewise generate certificate bundles. For connection certificates, the transport matters: the current injection map uses them for HTTPS and WSS connections. That is the point of declaring the requirement in the type metadata: Phoenix can ask for or generate the matching resource and block deployment when a required item is unresolved. It does not mean you should paste a private key or certificate into the public meta-file. Keep secrets in Phoenix’s protected vault/provisioning path, and let the deployment flow inject only what the agent needs. Use a constraint name the Phoenix version actually registers. If you invent a new one, you must also implement and register the editor or auto-generation handler. Otherwise the workspace can reject the agent before deployment—with the digital equivalent of “your paperwork is in a language we do not speak.” 4. Defaults, configuration editors, and panels Put ordinary operational defaults under config: polling intervals, paths, role names, safe-mode flags, or feature toggles. The MatrixOS agent should still validate values and apply defensive fallbacks; a default is not input validation wearing a nicer jacket. Phoenix has a useful fallback for configuration. When an operator double-clicks an agent node, it looks for a module named after the agent under config_editors and a class named in CamelCase. For shift_scribe, that means: matrix_gui/swarm_workspace/cls_lib/agent/config_editors/shift_scribe.py class ShiftScribe(...) If no specialized editor exists, Phoenix uses its generic editor for simple fields. A custom editor is worthwhile when the config needs typed controls, validation, grouped sections, or role pickers. Its save action should update the node’s config and mark the workspace dirty. A custom operations panel is a separate, optional module. Add its path to config.ui.panel, for example: "ui" : { "agent_tree" : { "emoji" : "🧭" }, "panel" : [ "shift_scribe.status_panel" ] } Then create matrix_gui/core/panel/custom_panels/shift_scribe/status_panel.py. Phoenix resolves that dotted path beneath custom_panels, imports the module, and looks for a class named StatusPanel. Custom panels implement the Phoenix panel interface and can contribute buttons or views for agent-specific operations. If you declare a panel path, ship the matching module and class; otherwise Phoenix will politely log that the panel is missing and continue without it. 5. Service roles are the command contract A service-manager entry advertises service roles and handlers that can be routed to the agent. It is not the custom panel itself. A simplified entry might look like: "service-manager" : [ { "role" : [ "shift_scribe.status@cmd_status" ], "scope" : [ "parent" , "any" ] } ] The agent must implement the matching handler, and any custom panel button that calls it must send a compatible service request. Think of the role string as the radio frequency: listing it in Phoenix does not install a radio in the agent. Keep the declared role, handler name, payload shape, and panel request aligned. The existing matrix_https manifest shows this pattern with perimeter toggle and status roles. Its config.ui.panel points to matrix_https.matrix_https; that path leads to a real custom panel, while service-manager lists the services it can request. One is the cockpit; the other is the set of commands it can call. They work together, but they are not interchangeable. 6. Put the two halves together and verify Before adding the new type to a real swarm, check the small integration contract: In MatrixOS, confirm the folder, init .py, module name, Agent class, imports, and lifecycle methods follow the existing agents under agents/python_core. In Phoenix, confirm agents_meta/shift_scribe.json parses and its filename, name, and MatrixOS package agree. Add the type in the Swarm Workspace palette. Confirm the icon appears, drag it into a test workspace, and inspect the constraints Phoenix loaded. Open its configuration. Check defaults, save an edit, and reopen it. If you declared a custom editor or panel, verify its module and CamelCase class load. Resolve the required constraints and deploy to a test environment. Verify the directive contains the intended config and provisioned fields, then confirm the worker logs, beacons, and service handlers behave as expected. If the agent is missing from the palette, begin with the JSON path and filename. If it appears but cannot be added, inspect the constraint registry. If the worker boots but behaves as though every setting is None, compare the editor’s saved config keys with the names read by the agent. If the panel button appears to salute and then do nothing, compare its service request with the role and handler that the agent actually registered. That is the whole handoff: MatrixOS owns behavior; Phoenix metadata describes how to assemble and operate the type; optional Phoenix modules provide richer editing and controls. The meta-file is not decorative paperwork. It is the map that gets the agent from “Python class exists” to “operator can add it, configure it, provision it, and use it.” Victory Always. 🌐 Links & Resources: MatrixOS source: https://github.com/matrixswarm/matrixos Phoenix source: https://github.com/matrixswarm/phoenix Try MatrixSwarm: https://matrixswarm.com Join the Community / Discord: https://discord.gg/2USbWVBVV YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMjiY4_-W2KP5fHXO0eC2ug

title: Building JC SRE NetProbe: A Python CLI for Network Health Checks, DevOps, and SRE
author: JacivaldoCarvalho
summary: Introduction As a Telecommunications Engineer interested in Networking, DevOps, and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), I've always been fascinated by how different layers of network infrastructure work together to deliver reliable services. When an application becomes unavailable, the problem isn't necessarily the application itself. It could be a DNS resolution issue, a TCP connection failure, an expired TLS certificate, or an HTTP service returning an unexpected response. Understanding where the failure occurs is an important part of troubleshooting. With that in mind, I built JC SRE NetProbe , an open-source Python command-line tool designed to simplify network connectivity checks and basic service health diagnostics. 🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/jacivaldocarvalho/jc-sre-netprobe What is JC SRE NetProbe? JC SRE NetProbe is a lightweight Python package that provides network diagnostic utilities through a command-line interface (CLI) and a Python API. The project brings together several common network checks into a single tool, making it useful for telecommunications professionals, network engineers, DevOps teams, and SRE practitioners. Its main capabilities include: TCP connectivity checks with latency measurement DNS resolution checks HTTP/HTTPS endpoint health checks IPv4 and IPv6 network information TLS certificate validation and expiration information Configurable timeouts Structured JSON output Exit codes designed for automation The goal is straightforward: make network troubleshooting easier to execute, understand, and automate. Why I Built It In network operations and infrastructure troubleshooting, engineers often need to perform multiple checks to identify why a service is unavailable. For example, consider an API endpoint that suddenly stops responding. Several questions immediately come to mind: Is the hostname resolving correctly? Can a TCP connection be established? Is the TLS certificate valid? Is the HTTP endpoint responding as expected? Each question investigates a different part of the service delivery process. I wanted to create a Python tool that could perform these checks consistently while also providing structured results suitable for scripting and automation. JC SRE NetProbe is a practical project that connects my telecommunications background with software development and SRE practices. Getting Started JC SRE NetProbe requires Python 3.11 or newer . Install the package using pip: pip install jc-sre-netprobe Once installed, the CLI is available directly from your terminal. 1. Checking TCP Connectivity To verify whether a remote service accepts TCP connections: jc-sre-netprobe tcp github.com 443 This checks connectivity to GitHub on TCP port 443. TCP connectivity checks are useful when investigating service availability, firewall restrictions, and network connectivity problems. 2. Checking DNS Resolution DNS plays a critical role in connecting applications to network services. To check hostname resolution: jc-sre-netprobe dns github.com This helps determine whether a hostname can be resolved before investigating higher-level protocols. 3. Checking HTTP/HTTPS Services A successful TCP connection doesn't necessarily mean that an application is healthy. To perform an HTTP health check: jc-sre-netprobe http https://github.com This provides an application-layer check of the endpoint. 4. Inspecting TLS Certificates TLS certificates are essential for secure communication. Expired or invalid certificates can cause application failures even when the underlying network is operational. To inspect a server's TLS certificate: jc-sre-netprobe tls github.com You can also configure a timeout: jc-sre-netprobe tls github.com --timeout 3 5. Working with IPv4 and IPv6 Networks The tool also provides network information for IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges. For example: jc-sre-netprobe network 192.168.1.0/24 This functionality can be useful when working with IP addressing and network infrastructure. Designed for Automation One of the important aspects of JC SRE NetProbe is its ability to integrate with scripts and operational workflows. JSON Output For example: jc-sre-netprobe --json tls github.com Structured output makes it easier to consume results programmatically and integrate checks into other tools. Operational Exit Codes The CLI uses exit codes that can be interpreted by automation systems. Exit Code Meaning 0 Target is healthy or check succeeded 1 Target is unhealthy or unavailable 2 Invalid CLI usage or input For example: jc-sre-netprobe tcp github.com 443 echo $? This behavior makes the tool useful in shell scripts, CI/CD pipelines, and operational checks. Using JC SRE NetProbe with Python In addition to its CLI, the package provides a Python API. For example, a TCP connectivity check can be performed directly from Python: from jc_sre_netprobe import tcp_check result = tcp_check ( " github.com " , 443 ) print ( result ) TLS checks are also available: from jc_sre_netprobe import tls_check result = tls_check ( " github.com " ) print ( result ) This allows developers to reuse the network probing functionality inside their own applications and automation scripts. Development and Code Quality Beyond implementing network checks, I wanted this project to follow good Python development practices. The repository includes: Ruff for linting Mypy for static type checking Pytest for automated testing Coverage for test coverage analysis GitHub Actions for CI/CD PyPI Trusted Publishing for package releases The CI pipeline validates the project against Python 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13. These practices help make the project more maintainable and provide a foundation for future improvements. Networking Meets Site Reliability Engineering One of the aspects I enjoy most about this project is how it connects traditional networking concepts with modern SRE practices. In telecommunications and network engineering, troubleshooting frequently involves understanding protocols, connectivity, addressing, and service behavior. In SRE, these same concepts are essential for investigating reliability and availability. JC SRE NetProbe brings these perspectives together through lightweight black-box checks. It isn't intended to replace comprehensive monitoring and observability platforms. Instead, it provides focused diagnostic utilities that can complement existing operational workflows. What's Next? I plan to continue improving JC SRE NetProbe as I explore new ideas in network automation, Python development, DevOps, and SRE. Some areas worth exploring include additional diagnostic capabilities, improved automation integrations, and more examples of real-world usage. As an open-source project, feedback, suggestions, and contributions are welcome. Final Thoughts Building JC SRE NetProbe has been an opportunity to combine my telecommunications engineering background with my interest in software development and infrastructure reliability. I believe that building practical tools is one of the best ways to deepen technical knowledge while contributing something useful to the community. If you work with networking, telecommunications, DevOps, or SRE, I'd love to hear your thoughts. What network diagnostic checks do you use most frequently in your daily work? Feel free to explore the repository, open an issue, or contribute. ⭐ GitHub: https://github.com/jacivaldocarvalho/jc-sre-netprobe Thanks for reading! Jacivaldo Carvalho Telecommunications Engineer | Networking | DevOps | SRE

title: Verify a company by name in 3 API calls (curl + Python)
author: Data Galactica
summary: Sunny Mittal works on marketing at Data Galactica. This post compares Data Galactica with other tools using each vendor's public pages as of the publish date; corrections welcome. Onboarding forms collect a company name, and company names are messy. "Infosys Ltd", "INFOSYS LIMITED" and "Infosys" might be the same company, or they might not. In this tutorial we'll take a typed name and go to a single verified record in three HTTP calls, using the Data Galactica API. Each call is shown with curl and with Python. Step 0: get a key Sign up at datagalactica.com/signup with your e-mail address and the code it sends you. The account is approved straight away, and your first key comes with â‚¹50 of free credit, which the API page says is about 312 calls. After that, each answered call costs â‚¹0.16 from a prepaid wallet. Errors and not-found answers are free, and so are a few lookup endpoints, including the one in Call 1. export DG_API_KEY = "your_key_here" The base URL is https://api.datagalactica.com/api/v1 , and the key goes in an Authorization: Bearer header. Call 1 (free): see who shares the name Before you verify anything, see how many records share the name. /suggest is a free typeahead endpoint and doesn't need a key: curl "https://api.datagalactica.com/api/v1/suggest?q=infosys&type=company" The first three results when I ran it: DGC-8SFS42RSWAX9 gold Infosys Limited Bangalore, India DGC-QH4XM7Q9189S bronze Infosys Kolkata, India DGC-36DSG3SV65YH bronze Infosys Faridabad, India This is the whole reason to verify. All three are called "Infosys", and only one is the IT company. The grade (bronze, silver, gold, verified) describes the contact details the registry holds, not whether two records are the same entity. Data Galactica's own notes for developers say exactly this, and use these Infosys records as the example. To tell records apart, use the place, the identifiers and the sources. DGC- means an organisation and DGP- means a person. A Galactica ID doesn't change once it's issued. Call 2: verify what the customer typed /verify/company takes the typed name plus whatever else you have (country, city, website) and returns a verdict: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $DG_API_KEY " \ "https://api.datagalactica.com/api/v1/verify/company?name=Infosys+Ltd&country=IN&website=infosys.com" A trimmed response, from the API documentation: { "ok" : true , "data" : { "verdict" : "match" , "confidence" : 1 , "operating" : true , "match" : { "id" : "DGC-8SFS42RSWAX9" , "name" : "Infosys Limited" , "status" : "operating" , "quality" : "gold" }, "checks" : { "name" : { "ok" : true , "score" : 1 }, "country" : { "ok" : true }, "website" : { "ok" : true } }, "candidates" : [ ... ] } } Three fields matter here. verdict gives the answer, checks shows which of your fields agreed, and operating tells you whether the company is still trading. If the verdict is possible_match , the developer guidance is to show the candidates to a person and stop, not to pick one automatically. Call 3: fetch the full record by Galactica ID Store the ID, not the name. Then fetch the record: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $DG_API_KEY " \ "https://api.datagalactica.com/api/v1/company/DGC-8SFS42RSWAX9" { "ok" : true , "data" : { "id" : "DGC-8SFS42RSWAX9" , "name" : "Infosys Limited" , "status" : "operating" , "founded" : "1981-07-02" , "identifiers" : { "cin" : "L85110KA1981PLC013115" , "lei" : "335800TYLGG93MM7PR89" , "wikidata" : "Q26989" }, "quality" : { "overall" : "gold" } } } The same endpoint accepts other identifiers in place of the Galactica ID. /company/L85110KA1981PLC013115 (the Indian CIN) gets you the same record, and so do the LEI, a UK company number, a US SEC CIK or a Wikidata ID. So if your CRM stores CINs and your finance system stores LEIs, both resolve to one key. All three calls in Python import os , sys , requests BASE = " https://api.datagalactica.com/api/v1 " KEY = os . environ . get ( " DG_API_KEY " ) # from datagalactica.com/signup HEADERS = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { KEY } " } if KEY else {} def get ( path , ** params ): r = requests . get ( f " { BASE }{ path } " , params = params , headers = HEADERS , timeout = 30 ) body = r . json () if not body . get ( " ok " ): sys . exit ( f " { r . status_code } { body [ ' error ' ][ ' code ' ] } : { body [ ' error ' ][ ' message ' ] } " ) return body [ " data " ] # Call 1 (free, no key): which records share this name? for hit in get ( " /suggest " , q = " infosys " , type = " company " )[ " results " ][: 3 ]: print ( hit [ " id " ], hit [ " grade " ], hit [ " name " ], " | " , hit [ " place " ]) # Call 2 (billed): verify the company the customer typed v = get ( " /verify/company " , name = " Infosys Ltd " , country = " IN " , website = " infosys.com " ) print ( v [ " verdict " ], v [ " confidence " ], v [ " match " ][ " id " ], v [ " operating " ]) # Call 3 (billed): full record by Galactica ID (a CIN or LEI works too) c = get ( f " /company/ { v [ ' match ' ][ ' id ' ] } " ) print ( c [ " name " ], c [ " status " ], c [ " identifiers " ]) If you run it without a key, Call 1 still prints, and the script then stops cleanly on the 401 api_key_required error with a link to sign up. I checked that behaviour before publishing. In production, handle 402 insufficient_balance the same way: the API returns it when the prepaid wallet is empty. Things to keep in mind Names collide. Treat a single name match as unconfirmed until place or an identifier agrees. Cite the ID. Data Galactica asks that answers cite the Galactica ID and the record's page URL. People records are sensitive. The registry also holds records about people. If you're curious what it holds about you, the Galactica Check page shows your own records after you confirm a code sent to your e-mail, and lets you correct, hide or remove them. That's it: one free call to see the ambiguity, one to resolve it, one to fetch the record. For bulk clean-up, the same API has /match , which takes up to 25 CRM rows per call and is billed per row matched. Sunny Mittal works on marketing at Data Galactica. title: Turning a messy payments export into a 2026 1099 vendor worksheet (without silently wrong totals)
author: Peter (The Trillium Company)
summary: For 2026 payments, the Form 1099-NEC reporting threshold goes from USD 600 to USD 2,000 (1099-MISC thresholds still vary by payment type, and backup withholding can require reporting below a threshold; see the IRS page ). If you keep the books for a small business, or write scripts for someone who does, this year's vendor list needs a fresh pass. The awkward part isn't the threshold; it's the export. Here's a small, defensive way to turn a messy payments export into a reviewable vendor worksheet. This is data preparation, not tax advice. The problems in a typical export The same vendor appears as Acme Plumbing LLC , ACME PLUMBING and Acme Plumbing, L.L.C. QuickBooks reports (e.g. Transaction List by Vendor ) put title lines above the header, put the vendor name on its own "group" row, and add Total for … rows, which double-count if you sum naively Dates in several formats, some blank or TBD Amounts like $1,200.00 , (450.00) and -$75 Payments from other years mixed in Rules that keep the totals honest Find the real header row. Skip leading lines until a row has at least two header-like cells (date, amount, name, vendor, memo). Inherit the vendor from group rows and skip Total for / TOTAL rows . Group by vendor ID if you have one; otherwise by exact name (case, punctuation and spacing normalised). Don't merge Acme LLC and Acme Inc automatically. Flag them as possible same vendor and let a human confirm. Never guess a date. Unparseable or missing dates go to a review list, not into the year's total. Never drop a bad amount silently. Invalid amounts go to the review list too. Reconcile. Input total = this year's total + other years + review rows. If that doesn't hold, stop. Report TIN presence, not TIN values. The worksheet only needs a yes/no. title: Vibe-Trading Hit 36K Stars in Six Months. I Read the Repo So You Don't Have To.
author: Toby Water
summary: Disclosure: This article was researched and drafted with AI assistance, then reviewed and edited by a human. All figures below are taken from the project's public GitHub page as of October 23, 2026. Every few months, a GitHub repo shows up that makes the whole "AI trading" corner of the internet lose its mind. This time it's Vibe-Trading (github.com/HKUDS/Vibe-Trading), from HKUDS, the data science lab at the University of Hong Kong, billed as "your personal trading agent." The numbers are not hype-sized, they're verifiable: created on April 1, 2026, the repo has passed 36,300 stars and 5,800 forks , with 3,324 commits from 33+ contributors and a release cadence that is close to daily — v0.1.18 shipped on October 22. In a space where the typical "AI hedge fund" repo has 40 commits and a README written like a movie trailer, that maintenance profile alone is worth a closer look. So I read it properly. Here's what it actually is, where the real value sits, and why the most interesting part of the project is the part its own authors tell you to be careful with. What It Actually Is Vibe-Trading is an open-source (MIT) research and trading-agent framework in Python. Strip away the branding and you get four components: A self-improving trading agent that runs research loops — pulling market data, forming hypotheses, testing them, and keeping what works in memory across sessions. Multi-agent "trading teams" — specialized agents (research, analysis, risk, execution support) that collaborate on a workflow instead of one model doing everything in a single chat. A cross-market data and backtesting layer , including a built-in library of 478 alpha factors you can test, combine, and inspect. A Shadow Account / paper trading setup — simulated execution against live-ish data, so strategies can run forward without real money on the line. It ships with multiple install paths (PyPI one-liner, Docker, an MCP plugin so other agents can call it as a tool), connectors for various brokers and data sources, and a web UI. This is not a prompt pack with a landing page. It's a working codebase with the boring infrastructure — session memory, scheduled research, an API server, security defaults — that real tools need and demo projects skip. Why It Grew So Fast Three reasons, I think. First, timing. "Let an agent watch the market for me" is the fantasy every retail trader has had since LLMs got tool use. Vibe-Trading is one of the first open-source projects to package that fantasy into something you can actually pip install . Second, credibility by contrast. The repo's competitors in the trending lists are often one-person marketing exercises — thousands of stars, a few dozen commits, promises of fully autonomous profit. HKUDS is a university lab with a track record, the contributor graph is real, and the changelog reads like a product being built, not a token being promoted. Third, the paper-trading-first design. The headline feature isn't "it trades for you." It's that you can run strategies in simulation, watch the agent's reasoning, and inspect the factor library. That's immediately useful to students, quant-curious developers, and small teams — a much bigger audience than people willing to hand an LLM their brokerage credentials. Where the Real Value Is If you strip out every trading fantasy, three things remain genuinely valuable: The factor library as a curriculum. 478 documented alpha factors is, functionally, a free course in quantitative strategy design. Reading how factors are defined, categorized, and combined teaches you more about systematic trading than a month of YouTube. Even if you never run a single backtest for production, the repo is a reference implementation of ideas that are usually locked inside textbooks and paywalled courses. Paper trading as a discipline tool. Most retail losses come from strategies that were never forward-tested at all. A shadow account forces the honest workflow: write the idea down, let it run against data you didn't cherry-pick, read the results. The agent layer makes that loop cheaper to run consistently — scheduled research, journaling, and cross-session memory mean the experiment actually continues instead of dying after one enthusiastic weekend. The multi-agent workflow pattern. Dividing research, risk-checking, and reporting across cooperating agents with tool contracts is a pattern that transfers far beyond trading. If you build internal tools for any small team, the architecture — agents with scoped tools, structured handoffs, human approval gates — is the part worth stealing. The MCP surface. Vibe-Trading also ships as an MCP plugin, which means other agent environments can call its research and backtesting tools directly instead of treating it as a standalone app you babysit. That's a quiet but important design decision: the project is positioning itself as infrastructure inside the broader agent ecosystem, not just a destination. Tools that plug into other people's workflows tend to outlive tools that demand to be the workflow — and it's one more reason the repo's growth looks structural rather than accidental. The Part the Authors Themselves Flag Here's the detail that separates this project from the grift end of the AI-trading pool: its own Disclaimer is blunt. Live trading through broker connectors is described by the project as experimental and not validated on real brokerage accounts, and the codebase reflects that caution. There's a TAP mode — full credential isolation with human-approved writes — meaning the agent can prepare an action but a person has to approve it before anything touches a real account. There's a /halt switch for the live runner. These are the design choices of people who understand exactly how this can go wrong. Take the hint. An LLM-driven agent with execution permissions is an operational risk even when the strategy is sound: malformed orders, runaway loops, costs you didn't model. The project's SECURITY file also warns that scammers have already issued fake tokens using the Vibe-Trading name — the project has no token, and anything claiming otherwise is fraud. If a "community" or "presale" attaches itself to this repo's brand, walk away. My rule, and the one I'd suggest to anyone experimenting: paper trade until the strategy has survived months of forward data and your own skepticism, and treat any live deployment as an engineering risk decision, not a vibe. Three Sane Ways to Use It 1. Learn factors, properly. Clone the repo, work through the factor library, reproduce a few backtests, and break them on purpose. Cheapest quant education available right now. 2. Run a shadow portfolio. Pick a simple strategy, let it paper trade, and review the agent's research notes weekly. You'll learn more about your own decision-making than about the market — which is the actual bottleneck for most people. 3. Borrow the workflow, not the trades. Use the multi-agent research pattern — data pull, hypothesis, test, report, human gate — inside your own team for market monitoring, competitor tracking, or content research. The trading is the demo; the workflow is the product. Vibe-Trading is still pre-1.0 software (v0.1.x), moving fast, and it will break in places. But it's the rare AI-trading project where the honest summary is more impressive than the hype: a well-maintained open-source lab for systematic research, built by people who put the warnings in the README themselves. I run Tobywater Digital, where we help small teams deploy and actually operate open-source AI tooling — including research workflows like this one — with the boring parts (setup, guardrails, human approval gates) done properly. If you'd like a guided setup or a paper-trading workflow configured for your team, that's the kind of deployment work we do. No return promises, no trade calls — just tooling that runs.

title: ByBet Casino: A Closer Look at Its Mobile Gaming Experience
author: Kenneth Atienza
summary: A casino page may look sharp on a phone, yet smooth use needs more than bright tiles . Small screens make menu size, load time, and cash status harder to judge than desktop pages. For Filipino adults aged 21+ , these details matter when game sites handle both money and private data. The ByBet Casino website says its games and account pages work on phones and tablets. It lists slots, live tables, promotions, and banking , though its speed claims lack public test results. This review studies mobile user experience through public pages, without claiming access to private test data. Mobile Friendly Claims Need More Than A Label The homepage calls its mobile pages easy to use and quick to load on many phones. It also claims that smaller screens retain key features, including game menus and banking tools . Those are site claims, not proof of quick loads on each phone or mobile network. A good phone review asks whether tabs stay clear when screens turn narrow or tall. Text should stay easy to read without zoom, while tabs should respond to light taps . A layout that fits one phone may still fail on another screen or browser version. The site's Login and Register links lead to bybet.com , not to an account page here. That change shows the guide and account service play distinct roles for people who use phones. A safe handoff needs a clear web address , so users know which site now gets their data. Touch Menus Reveal Problems That Desktop Screens Hide ByBet's homepage groups slot games, live casino games, and specialty games under separate page sections. On small screens, large tap zones and clear labels help users tell these groups apart. A bright game tile is not enough if nearby controls are too small to select. A good test would check scrolling, back links, and page shifts without making any paid bets. Tests should cover screen turns and text size changes , which can push tabs out of view. No published test proves those checks pass , so claims about the design still need real proof. Live Casino Video Adds Pressure To Weak Connections The site lists live blackjack, baccarat, and roulette alongside its main groups of slot games. Unlike still images, live video needs a steady stream to keep a dealer in clear view. A clear picture does not prove a bet was accepted , since video and wager logs differ. When data drops, the screen may lag while a game server keeps its own round log . The player may see a late frame, though the account could show a settled round already . A late screen is not proof of a changed result , which needs a full log check. For coders, network tests should track failed loads, long pauses, and switches from WiFi to data . A good report must state the phone and network used , not claim fast speeds for all. The site does not publish such test logs , so its speed claims remain unproved in this review. Payment Screens Need Clear Status And Error Messages The homepage names GCash, Maya, and bank transfers as ways to move funds in the Philippines. A phone cashier should show whether a payment is pending, done, or declined after each request. A wallet charge alone does not prove the game balance changed , as two systems hold separate logs. A good error screen needs a clear status and reference code , without showing private account data. Small screens should keep cancel and retry taps far apart , to cut the risk of mistakes. No live cashier test was done here , so the site's cash claims lack direct checks. Phone Browsers Carry Privacy And Session Risks The site's privacy page says it may gather device type, browser details, IP address, and cookies . It also lists account, cash, and game activity data , which could put private details at risk. A privacy policy states intended rules , but cannot prove all safeguards work in real life. On a shared phone, saved logins and browser history may leave account clues in sight for others. Moving from the guide to the account site can also change the web address shown . The full domain matters more than a logo , mainly before users type a password or code. The homepage has an age notice for adults over 21 , plus links to safer play guidance. Those links explain age rules and support , but do not prove live checks of a person's age. An age popup does not replace ID checks , and mobile ease must not weaken those steps. Developers Can Test The Journey Without Guessing Results A fair test starts with a small screen, slow data, and clear notes on each page change . It checks tap size, text wrap, and load states , rather than treating bright icons as proof. Test results should name the phone and date , since sites and phone software can change. Another test tracks the jump from guide page to login page , and notes each web address. It should flag strange redirects and missing error text , but should never store real account secrets. An open guide page cannot prove private account behavior , which would need a separate test. It checks page-wide horizontal overflow at three mobile viewport widths without logging into accounts or placing bets. Results have not been collected, and passing this check alone does not establish full mobile accessibility. Public Claims And Verified Experience Must Stay Separate The site presents mobile access as a core feature , but posts no public phone test report. That leaves load speed and live table stability as open questions, not as proven strengths. A developer review must separate site claims from test results , or it becomes sales copy. For readers, game menus, account pages, and payment screens need distinct checks on each phone. Fast menus do not prove instant cashouts , and smooth reels do not verify a game provider's license. Good mobile design means clear states and honest limits , not a promise of wins or safety. The ByBet Casino mobile gaming section describes access through phones, tablets, and the site's main features. Its public claims cover game menus and banking access , but lack independent phone speed tests . The main point remains: phone access is advertised, yet public tests do not prove claimed speeds.

title: I'm building Mocxam: a white-label mock test platform for coaching institutes
author: Arun
summary: At Ceptor Labs, we build software for problems we see up close. Today we're introducing Mocxam , a platform that lets coaching institutes launch their own branded online test series, without building software themselves. The problem we set out to solve Preparing for SSC, Banking, Railways or UPSC means taking a lot of mock tests. Behind most of those tests, a coaching institute is doing manual work: Questions live in documents and spreadsheets. Tests run on generic form tools with no real exam feel. There's often no negative marking, no section timers and no proper question palette. Students get a score, but no idea why they lost marks. The institute's own brand barely shows up. Large test-prep platforms cover parts of this, but the institute ends up promoting someone else's brand. Small and mid-sized institutes want their own name, their own students and their own data. Mocxam is built for them. What Mocxam gives an institute Each institute gets a coaching dashboard for staff and a branded student portal for candidates. The coaching dashboard Control Room: plan usage, student seats and quick actions on one screen. Mock Test Studio: create tests, set duration and marking, and publish or disable them with one click. Question bank and editor: tag each question by exam, subject and difficulty, with a live preview of what students will see. AI Paper Setter: draft question papers with AI. Institutes can bring their own Gemini key. [Add: how this works in practice.] Bulk imports: enrol students with one CSV (name, email, password) and import questions by CSV, with a row-by-row validation report. Exam syllabi and marking: set the marking scheme once per exam and it applies to every mock. Faculty and role-based access: staff accounts with different permissions. Audit trail and academy settings: a record of changes, plus logo, colours and font. The student portal Candidates sign in to a portal that carries the institute's name and colours. They can: Take full-length, sectional or topic-wise tests with real timing and negative marking. Use a distraction-free test player with a question palette, flags and a live timer. See instant results with accuracy per section and topic. Review step-by-step solutions for every question. Mistake analysis: the feature we care about most A score alone doesn't help a student improve. After each test, Mocxam labels wrong answers so students know what to change: Silly mistakes: they knew it, but slipped. Concept gaps: the topic needs another look. Time sinks: questions that used too much of the clock. This turns a mock test from a scoreboard into practice. Design decisions behind it One institute, one portal. Every institute gets its own student portal on its own subdomain, with separate admin and student entry points. Candidate data is kept isolated per institute, which matters when institutes compete with each other. White-label by default. Logo, colours, favicon and font are settings, not custom work. Higher plans can remove "Powered by Mocxam" entirely. Imports come first. Institutes already hold thousands of questions and hundreds of students. If onboarding means retyping them, nobody switches. So we made CSV import with clear validation errors a core feature. Exam-faithful practice. A mock test only helps if it feels like the real exam, so marking schemes and timers are configured per exam. Plans Plans start with a free pilot (up to 25 students and 2 mock tests) and scale through Starter, Academy Pro and Institution Scale. What we learned building it Onboarding is the product. Bulk import was the first thing institutes asked about. White-label is mostly small details. Favicons, footers, emails and login pages all need to carry the institute's brand. Students want the "why". Per-topic accuracy and mistake labels get more attention than the raw score. Try Mocxam Mocxam is free to start. If you run or work with a coaching institute, we'd love your feedback. Website: https://coaching.mockbazaar.com/ Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XLOViAWZTzs Contact: proxyceptor@gmail.com Have you built something similar, or taken these mock tests as a student? Tell us in the comments what you'd want most. Mocxam is built by Ceptor Labs .
